subject: electric catfish
title: This Catfish Fires 350 Volts, and Egyptians Carved It 5,000 Years Ago

scenes.text: This catfish can hit you with 350 volts.
The electric catfish of the Nile and other African rivers. Up to 1.2 metres long and around 20 kilograms.
It hunts by stunning: one discharge and the fish around it go limp. Short volleys drive off anything that comes too close.
For a human it's painful, not fatal. The ancient Egyptians knew it well: it appears in tomb reliefs more than 5,000 years old.
Fishing scenes in the tomb of Ty at Saqqara are among the earliest known pictures of any electric animal.
Its old Egyptian name meant roughly: the one who saved many in the sea. Grab one, drop the whole net, and you'd understand.

description:
The electric catfish of Africa can discharge up to 350 volts, and ancient Egyptians carved it into tomb walls more than 5,000 years ago.
Malapterurus electricus grows to about 1.2 m and roughly 20 kg. It stuns prey with its discharge and fires short volleys at intruders; the shock is painful to humans but not known to be fatal. It appears in Old Kingdom fishing reliefs such as those in the mastaba of Ty at Saqqara, among the earliest known depictions of the fish, and one Egyptian name for it translates roughly as the one who had saved many in the sea.
Which would you rather meet in the water: this, or an electric eel?
first_comment: Egyptian fishermen were drawing this fish before the pyramids. Which animal do you think humans have feared the longest?
